title: Probabilistic forecasting of replication studies

selection.evidence: Chosen 2026-11-05 to test a hypothesis of mine: per-study shrinkage forecasts are miscalibrated because they ignore selection on significance. Ships data + code (R package ReplicationSuccess). Prior suspicion of the paper: none.

cost.compute_notes: PLoS PDF (23 pp, read pp 1-20). ReplicationSuccess 1.3.3 from CRAN: RProjects.rda (143 pairs), SSRP.rda, protzko2020.rda read with pyreadr. Python re-implementation of eqs 2-6 (p01); known-answer worlds 5 x 100 projects (p02, 75 s); selection-aware NPMLE forecaster (selection_forecast.py) on the 4 projects (p03); 7 data-generating worlds incl. p-hacking (p04, 125 s). Out-of-sample on FReD in the roseler2024 record (f01-f04).

triggers: forecast replication outcome from original study p-value and sample size
is a replication forecast calibrated Brier Spiegelhalter
prediction market vs statistical forecast replication
do larger replications succeed more often
selection on significance shrinkage empirical Bayes original effect inflated
replication project RPP EERP SSRP experimental philosophy data

claims.statement: Forecasts that take the original estimate at face value (N: flat prior, tau = 0) overestimate the number of significant replications in all four projects: expected 15.0 / 27.8 / 55.4 / 19.9 vs observed 11 / 23 / 24 / 13 (economics n = 18, philosophy 31, psychology 73, social sciences 21).
claims.scope: One-to-one replication projects on the Fisher-z scale, sigma = 1/sqrt(n-3); 'significant' = two-sided p < .05 in the original direction.

quantities.name: naive_brier_psychology
quantities.baseline: reproduced 0.394; econ .271, phil .193, soc .346 all reproduce

our_assessment.why: Re-implemented from the equations in Python; every expected count, Brier score, coverage and Spiegelhalter z in Tables 2-3 and Fig 7 reproduces to the printed digit for all four methods (after fixing an ordering bug of my own in the S method).

claims.statement: Evidence-based shrinkage plus heterogeneity (SH, tau = 0.08) performs best of the four statistical methods everywhere and is calibrated in economics (12.4 expected vs 11) and philosophy (24.1 vs 23), but not in psychology (45.9 vs 24, Spiegelhalter z 5.2) or social sciences (17.6 vs 13, z 3.4). 'Good predictive performance in two of the four data sets.'
claims.scope: tau fixed a priori at 0.08 (Cohen-classification argument, 34th percentile of 497 Psych Bull meta-analyses).

quantities.name: SH_normalised_brier_philosophy
quantities.baseline: best value in the paper; reproduced

our_assessment.why: Reproduces exactly. The 'two of four' that are well calibrated are the two smallest projects (n = 18, 31), where Spiegelhalter's test has the least power; the larger out-of-sample test (FReD, 1,082 pairs, c7) does not show calibration for any method.

claims.statement: Prediction markets beat every statistical forecast in the social sciences project (Brier .114 vs SH .272, perfect separation) and match the shrinkage methods in economics (.243).
claims.scope: Two projects with markets, n = 18 and 21.

our_assessment.why: Reproduces. Markets see things the statistical model cannot (plausibility, prior failures, the effect's reputation); the FReD result (c7) -- original |t| carries little and replication n none of the signal -- is the same fact from the other side.

claims.statement: HYPOTHESIS (mine, before running): SH is miscalibrated in psychology because per-study shrinkage cannot see selection on significance. REFUTED by known-answer worlds at RPP's own (n_o, n_r): with honest selection on |t_o| > 1.96 and no heterogeneity, SH is roughly calibrated (half-null world: expected 49.9 vs observed 50.6; 80%-null world: 46.9 vs 41.4), so selection alone cannot open RPP's gap of 45.9 vs 24.
claims.scope: 5 worlds x 100 simulated projects of 73 pairs; true effects normal around r = .3 or zero; one-sided selection on two-sided significance.

our_assessment.why: My hypothesis, tested on worlds where the answer is known, and it failed: SH's evidence-based shrinkage absorbs most of what selection does at these sample sizes. Kept here so the idea is not re-proposed.

claims.statement: A selection-aware forecaster (NPMLE of the true-effect distribution across a project's originals, likelihood truncated at |t| > 1.96) lowers the overprediction in psychology (SH 45.9 -> 40.1 at tau .08, 39.0 at tau .15) and economics (10.0-10.4 vs 11 observed), but loses discrimination (psychology AUC .70 -> .61; philosophy Brier .148 -> .233, AUC .80 -> .54) and is worse than SH out-of-sample on FReD (AUC .557 vs .579). Not an improvement.
claims.scope: Per-project NPMLE on 16-65 significant originals, grid of 221 Fisher-z values; FReD fit on 878 significant originals.

our_assessment.why: Recorded as a failed method. A spiky NPMLE on a few dozen originals turns every forecast into a function of n_r alone; the per-study rule keeps the ordering information that the pooled prior throws away. In p02's selected worlds the same forecaster had the lowest Brier score -- it fails on real data, not on its own assumptions.

claims.statement: Which worlds DO reproduce RPP's pattern? p-hacking (first significant of 5 correlated analyses) with 80% null originals: observed 26.8 vs SH 42.1; all-true small effects (r ~ .1): 25.1 vs 37.9. But both bunch 54-56% of |t_o| in (1.96, 2.5), and RPP's originals bunch 34%. A replication-side attenuation world (true replication effect = half the original's) gives 31.0 vs 50.9 with 23% bunching. RPP's gap is better matched by attenuation at replication than by a p-hacking signature in the originals.
claims.scope: 7 worlds x 100 projects at RPP's design; bunching = share of originals with 1.96 < |t_o| < 2.5. Coarse discrimination between mechanisms, not an estimate of their shares.

quantities.name: rpp_original_bunching_share_1.96_2.5
quantities.baseline: honest half-null world .278; p-hacked 80%-null world .555; attenuation world .233

our_assessment.why: A simulation discrimination between a handful of mechanisms. It says the information about RPP's failures is not visible in the originals' z-distribution, which agrees with the FReD finding that original |t| carries little signal (roseler2024 c3). It cannot separate 'true decline' from 'replications differ from originals' (heterogeneity of method).

claims.statement: Out of sample on FReD (1,082 original-replication pairs, 475 originals, blinded copy): SH expects 638.5 significant replications, 388 observed (36%); best variant (SH, tau = .2) 504.9. Discrimination: AUC .579 against a ceiling of .839 [.819, .858] if SH were the data-generating process. The model's backbone -- larger replications succeed more -- fails: log(n_r/n_o) has AUC .472 alone and logit coefficient -0.05 (SE .075), where SH implies AUC .66 [.64, .69].
claims.scope: Outcome = replication p <= .05 and not coded 'failed'; c approximated from n (exact for correlations only); originals' |t| from exact p (747) or a parsed 1-df statistic (335). Robust in every subset tried (exact-p only, parsed only, first replication per original, 1/k weights, no mega-replications, significant originals only).

quantities.name: fred_logit_coef_log_nr_over_no
quantities.baseline: SE 0.075 (clustered by original), p = .47; log|t_o| coef 0.747 (SE .203)

our_assessment.why: The paper's conclusion that SH predicts well in two of four projects does not generalise to the largest open set of replications. The deficit is not mainly calibration-in-the-large (tau can fix the count) but discrimination: the two inputs the model uses carry little (|t_o|) or no (n_r) information. A two-class reading (a share of nulls) fitted by ML degenerates (tau -> infinity, pi = .30), i.e. the model family itself is wrong for these data.

datasheet.composition: one row per original-replication pair; effects on correlation and Fisher-z scale with SEs from n; p-values two- and one-sided; prediction-market belief where it exists (EE, SS).
datasheet.caveats: Psychology = RPP meta-analytic subset (73 of 100). The package's protzko2020 data is from Protzko et al., whose Nature Human Behaviour paper (2023) was retracted in 2024 -- do not use it as evidence of high replicability.

artifacts.locator: ReplicationSuccess R/powerSignificance.R (designPrior = 'EB' is the SH model)

checked.how: read; formula compared line by line with my selection_forecast.p_sig_pawel
checked.result: Identical: s = max(1 - (1+h)/zo^2, 0), mu = s zo sqrt(c), sigma^2 = s c (1+h) + 1 + h c.

relations.why: Out-of-sample test of this paper's forecasts (c7) uses FReD.
Same session: a detector is calibrated in known-answer worlds before it is applied.
Both read a gap between observed and model-expected agreement as evidence about the world, when the gap is first a statement about the null/forecast model's family.

open_questions: FReD has closeness_* codings (instructions, measures, stimuli, participants...) -- do they carry the signal that |t_o| and n_r do not? That is the direct test of the heterogeneity explanation (c6). Not yet run.
Reproduce Roeseler (2023) 'Predicting replication rates with z-curve' (osf.io/ewb2t) on the same blinded FReD copy: is z-curve's ERR calibrated where SH is not?
After mark unblinds: remove the f00 blinding filter and check that no conclusion changes.
